P000 00:00:01 S1: Let's start with the set piece, because that is where your teams are known.
P001 00:00:11 S2: The scrum is a contest of angles before it is a contest of strength. If the tight head's shoulder is above his hip the pressure goes nowhere. We film every scrum from behind the posts so the players see their own body height.
P002 00:00:41 S1: How much of that is coachable and how much is simply size?
P003 00:00:49 S2: Size buys you a margin, but technique is what survives eighty minutes. Our lightest prop last season won more penalties than anyone in the league. He did it by getting his bind earlier than the man opposite him.
P004 00:01:16 S1: And the line-out, is that a different skill entirely?
P005 00:01:23 S2: The line-out is a timing problem dressed up as a jumping problem. The lifters have to be moving before the hooker's hands leave the ball. We drill the call to the throw in under two seconds, every session.
P006 00:01:50 S1: Do you change the calls much during a match?
P007 00:01:57 S2: We carry four and we use two, because a caller who is thinking is a caller who is late. The opposition scout our first six line-outs and we know that they do. So the sixth one is usually the one we have been saving.
P008 00:02:27 S1: What about the breakdown, which everyone says is where matches are won?
P009 00:02:36 S2: The breakdown rewards whoever arrives with their feet already set. A player who arrives fast and off balance gives away the penalty every time. We coach the last three steps before the ruck, not the sprint into it.
P010 00:03:03 S1: Is that why your penalty count dropped so sharply last year?
P011 00:03:12 S2: Partly, and partly because we stopped asking the flankers to compete on every ball. Choosing three rucks a half to attack is worth more than contesting thirty. The referee starts to trust a pack that is not always on the edge.
P012 00:03:41 S1: How do you decide which three?
P013 00:03:46 S2: We look for the ruck after a big carry, when their support is still getting up. That is the moment the ball is slowest and the guard is thinnest. Everything else we leave alone and get back into the defensive line.
P014 00:04:14 S1: Does any of this change on a wet night in February?
P015 00:04:22 S2: The weather changes the reward, not the method. In the wet the scrum is worth more because the backs will not run from deep. So we shorten the game and make them play in front of their own posts.
P016 00:04:49 S1: What do you look for when you recruit a young forward?
P017 00:04:57 S2: Work rate first, because you cannot teach a man to want the next collision. Then neck and shoulder strength, because that part takes the longest to build. Skills we can add, and we can add them quickly at that age.
P018 00:05:25 S1: What is the most common mistake you see in club rugby?
P019 00:05:33 S2: Packs that push straight when they should be pushing across. A straight shove against a good front row is a shove into a wall. The angle is free and almost nobody takes it.
P020 00:05:58 S1: I want to change subject completely, because you also write about money.
P021 00:06:07 S2: Compound interest is the one idea in finance that everybody agrees on. It works because the return itself starts earning a return of its own. The first ten years look disappointing and the last ten look like magic.
P022 00:06:34 S1: Why do people give up during the disappointing part?
P023 00:06:41 S2: Because the curve is almost flat there, and a flat curve feels like failure. A pound saved in the first year is worth many pounds saved in the twentieth. But it does not feel that way while you are saving it.
P024 00:07:09 S1: What do you tell someone starting at forty rather than at twenty?
P025 00:07:18 S2: That the arithmetic is harsher, but that it is not hopeless. They have to save a larger share and they have to leave it alone for longer. The mistake is deciding to make up the lost time with extra risk.
P026 00:07:46 S1: You mean picking individual stocks?
P027 00:07:51 S2: I mean anything at all that promises to shorten the wait. The wait is the product, and the return is what you are paid for enduring it. Every scheme that removes the wait puts something worse in its place.
P028 00:08:18 S1: So a broad index fund and nothing else?
P029 00:08:24 S2: For almost everybody, a broad index fund at a low fee is the whole answer. The fee matters more than people believe, because the fee compounds as well. One per cent a year for thirty years is a quarter of the final pot.
P030 00:08:54 S1: A quarter seems far too large to be true.
P031 00:09:00 S2: Run the numbers and it is worse than that in a low return decade. The fee is charged on the balance, so it grows exactly as your money grows. It is compound interest, working very patiently for somebody else.
P032 00:09:28 S1: What about timing the market at all, even a little?
P033 00:09:35 S2: The evidence is that missing the best twenty days ruins a thirty year record. And the best days sit right next to the worst days, which is the cruel part. You cannot avoid the one without also missing the other.
P034 00:10:03 S1: Do you rebalance the portfolio at all?
P035 00:10:09 S2: Once a year, on a date I picked in advance and do not move. The date matters far less than the fact that I did not choose it while watching news. A rule you wrote when you were calm is worth more than a decision made when you are not.
P036 00:10:42 S1: Is there anything here you have changed your mind about?
P037 00:10:50 S2: I used to think an emergency fund of three months was enough. I now think six, because its real job is to stop you selling at the bottom. It is not really a savings account, it is insurance against your own behaviour.
P038 00:11:19 S1: What would you tell a twenty year old today?
P039 00:11:26 S2: Automate it, keep the fee low, then go and spend your attention elsewhere. The plan does not need you once it is running. Watching it will only tempt you into breaking it.
